the rejection of trace organics by RO membranes can be described by the combined effects of steric and hydrophobic interactions, and the rejection of trace compounds by NF membranes can be described as a combined effect of steric, hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions.

the rejection of trace organics by high-pressure membranes is a function of compound properties, operational conditions (pH, ionic strength, temperature), and membrane properties (pore size, hydrophobicity, surface charge).
rejection of organic compounds by high pressure membranes can be explained based on compound properties (hydrophobicity and molecular size) and membrane properties (hydrophility and charge).

rejection of trace organic chemicals by high-pressure membranes is a complex process involving compound properties, membrane characteristics, and operational conditions, and that the current understanding of the mechanisms involved in the process is limited.

solute-membranes interactions are important in determining rejection of trace organic chemicals by high pressure membranes, and that these interactions can be characterized by diffusion measurements, in conjunction with other measurements.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the rejection of organic solutes by high-pressure membranes is governed by a combination of compound properties, including hydrophobicity and size, membrane properties, including pore structure, and operational parameters, including pressure and pH.
rejection of trace organic contaminants by high-pressure membranes is not simply related to compound hydrophobicity, and the rejection is not simply related the MWCO of the membrane.
the transport of trace organic compounds in high pressure membranes may be described by a combination of solute properties, solute-membranes interactions, and membrane properties.
